title: The 'Health Halo' Hustle: Why Your Avocado Oil Might Be a Cheap Imposter
summary: Picture this: you're at Whole Foods, reaching for a $10 bag of avocado-oil potato chips, feeling virtuous. But a new study from UC Davis suggests you might be paying a premium for a lie. Researchers chemically analyzed 54 products — chips, mayo, dressings — that listed avocado oil as their sole oil. A staggering 89% appeared to be cut with cheaper oils like sunflower or soybean. One contained no avocado oil at all. 'It's one of the more egregious recent examples of food mislabeling,' says NPR's Maria Godoy. But outright fraud is just the tip of the iceberg. The subtler — and perfectly legal — strategy is 'healthwashing': using buzzwords ('organic,' 'non-GMO,' 'high protein') and pastoral packaging to cast a 'health halo' over products that are still ultra-processed and sugar-laden. Behavioral economists point to asymmetric information: we buyers know far less about what's in our food than sellers do. That gap lets companies exploit our cognitive shortcuts. We see '100% avocado oil' and assume the whole product is wholesome — a classic halo effect. In reality, those chips might have the same nutritional profile as regular ones, just with a fancier label and a 300% markup. 'It's a pricing strategy,' explains food policy legend Marion Nestle. 'Companies know some consumers — typically those with more disposable income — will pay more for perceived health benefits.' The FDA requires ingredient lists, but enforcement is spotty, and most of us don't scrutinize fine print in a crowded aisle. The avocado oil study could spur tighter regulations. But Nestle, author of the upcoming book Sugar Coated, says the real defense is skepticism: 'Ignore the front of the package. Turn it around. If sugar or refined flour is in the first three ingredients, it's not a health food.' In a marketplace where even 'pure' isn't pure, the smartest shopper is a cynical one.
why_it_matters: For teenagers bombarded by social media food trends and influencer endorsements, recognizing healthwashing protects them from wasting money on fake 'superfoods.' It also builds critical reading skills that matter far beyond the snack aisle—learning to question marketing claims is a life skill.

background_read: Food fraud has a long history—olive oil, honey, and seafood are often stretched with cheaper alternatives because purity tests are expensive and enforcement is inconsistent. The FDA (the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the agency that regulates food labeling) requires ingredient lists, but the agency lacks the resources to verify every 'pure' claim on supermarket shelves.

Marion Nestle, a nutrition professor at New York University and author of the upcoming book *Sugar Coated*, has spent decades studying how food companies manipulate health claims. She notes that shoppers with more disposable income are particularly vulnerable to paying a premium for perceived benefits.

Behavioral economists call this a classic case of asymmetric information: sellers know exactly what's in the product, while buyers must rely on packaging cues—a situation that leads to the halo effect, where one positive attribute (like avocado oil) makes us overlook the rest of the ingredients.

perspectives.description: Companies that use genuinely pure avocado oil can gain customer loyalty if this scandal drives demand for verified products. Honest food brands could see a boost, and consumers who read labels become smarter, supporting transparency and quality.

This fraud cheats shoppers out of money they spend for health reasons, and it can undermine efforts to improve nutrition. When deception is widespread, it erodes public trust in all food labels, making it harder for truly healthy products to stand out.

Economists see asymmetric information as a classic reason why markets don't work perfectly. Without strong enforcement, companies have little incentive to be truthful, and consumers rely on heuristics like the halo effect—a cognitive pattern studied in behavioral science.

Public pressure could lead to tighter FDA testing and stricter fines for mislabeling. Innovations like blockchain-based supply chain tracking might one day let shoppers scan a code and see exactly what's in a product, making marketing tricks obsolete.
